# Brahāchattajātaka (Ja 336)

**ID:** Ja 336
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Chatta the Tall

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Brahāchattajātaka* (Ja 336) is a canonical birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection, rendered into English as *Chatta the Tall* [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha delivered the discourse while staying at Jetavana concerning a deceitful monk (*kuhaka*), with the opening verse beginning *Tiṇaṁ tiṇan ti lapasīti* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past set during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta served as a wise minister who acted as an advisor on both spiritual and worldly matters (*atthadhammānusāsako amacco*) [Fausböll 1883].

The narrative illustrates ancient royal education, recounting how Chatta, a son of the king of Kosala, fled to Taxila after his father was taken prisoner [Law 1926]. At Taxila, Prince Chatta mastered the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vijjā*), and learned the *nidhi-uddharaṇamanta*—a spell or science used for discovering hidden treasure—which enabled him to recover his deceased father's fortune [Law 1926]. At the conclusion of the discourse, the Buddha identifies the birth (*samodhāna*), stating that Chatta the Tall was reborn as the deceitful monk, while the Bodhisatta was the wise minister who counseled righteous rule [Fausböll 1883].

In V. Fausböll's edition of the Jātaka commentary, the tale is positioned in the third volume as the sixth story of its section, between the *Jambukajātaka* and the *Pīṭhajātaka* [Fausböll 1883]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects Pali-internal text reuse with the commentary in *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo) spanning six shared passages (473 characters; longest match §3.4–4.4 with §945–946), while identifying no cross-language matches in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora meeting its similarity threshold [DharmaNexus].
